It extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with a compact set of temporal parameters to model continuous-time motion [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with a compact set of temporal parameters to model continuous-time motion. The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] passages: 'we extend each static Gaussian with a compact set of temporal parameters' and 'This gives a continuous trajectory over the whole sequence instead of predicting a separate state for every frame.' The notes further confirm that the parameters include velocity, acceleration, canonical time, and log-duration, which are used to calculate position at any time t, thus modeling continuous-time motion.

*   **Temporal Support:** Dynamic Gaussians do not contribute to every frame; they appear/disappear smoothly around $t'_i$ based on $\sigma_i$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that dynamic Gaussians do not contribute to every frame and appear/disappear smoothly around $t'_i$ based on $σ_i$. The evidence explicitly supports this in the 'Soft Temporal Support' section: 'A dynamic Gaussian does not necessarily need to contribute to every frame... define its temporal weight as $w_i(t) = exp(-1/2 ((t - t'_i)/σ_i + ε)^2)$... so that static Gaussians always keep their original opacity, while dynamic Gaussians smoothly appear and disappear around their canonical time $t'_i$.' The formula for $w_i(t)$ depends on $t'_i$ and $σ_i$, confirming the mechanism described in the claim.

The note '[S1, unofficial]' in the claim likely refers to the interpretation of the limitation regarding complex deformations, which is supported by the text's emphasis on the simplicity and explicit nature of the motion model versus implicit networks.
